specPoints.text: describe how long-chain alkanes are converted to alkenes and shorter-chain alkanes by catalytic cracking (using silica or alumina as the catalyst and a temperature in the range of 600–700 ºC)
explain why cracking is necessary, in terms of the balance between supply and demand for different fractions

primer.text: From Crude Oil you already know how the column sorts molecules by chain length, and Combustion showed what happens when they burn. This note explains the industrial fix for the wrong-sized fractions: cracking long chains apart over a hot catalyst to make the short ones the market wants.

lessons.title: Breaking long chains on purpose
lessons.opening: Cracking is the deliberate breaking of long hydrocarbon chains into shorter, more useful ones. This lesson covers what the process is, the hot conditions it needs, and the mixture of products it always delivers.
keyPoints: Cracking breaks low-demand long-chain hydrocarbons into more useful short-chain molecules.
Kerosene and diesel are the usual feedstocks, cracked to give petrol, alkenes and hydrogen.
Catalytic cracking heats hydrocarbons to around 600 to 700 degrees Celsius to vaporise them.
The vapours pass over a hot powdered catalyst such as alumina or silica, whose surface breaks the covalent bonds.
The bond-breaking causes thermal decomposition reactions, producing a mixture of shorter alkanes and alkenes.

low.restatement: Cracking cuts long, unpopular hydrocarbon chains into short, wanted ones. The oil is vaporised at 600 to 700 degrees, passed over a hot catalyst, and the chains snap into shorter alkanes and alkenes. The catalyst surface is where the long chains actually snap.
low.analogy: It is like cutting a long rope into shorter pieces at a hot workbench: same rope, but now the lengths people actually want to buy.
low.examPointer: Quote both conditions, the temperature range and the hot powdered catalyst, whenever a question asks how cracking is done.

medium.restatement: In catalytic cracking, long-chain hydrocarbons are heated to around 600 to 700 degrees Celsius until they vaporise, then the vapours pass over a hot powdered catalyst such as alumina or silica. Contact with the catalyst surface breaks covalent bonds, so thermal decomposition reactions split each long chain randomly into a mixture of shorter alkanes and alkenes.
medium.analogy: Think of a hot metal comb dragged through tangled string: wherever the strands touch the hot teeth they snap, and one long string leaves as a bundle of assorted shorter lengths.
medium.examPointer: Name the catalyst material from the spec wording, silica or alumina, and describe the random split into both alkane and alkene products.

check.stem: What is the purpose of cracking?

options.text: To convert long-chain molecules into more useful short-chain molecules
options.explanation: Low-demand long chains are deliberately broken into the short chains the market wants.

options.text: To join short molecules into longer chains
options.explanation: That is the reverse of cracking; cracking only cuts chains down.

options.text: To remove sulfur impurities from the fuel
options.explanation: Impurity removal is not the aim; chain cutting is.

options.text: To test whether a hydrocarbon is an alkane
options.explanation: Cracking is an industrial process, not a chemical test.

check.stem: What temperature range is used for catalytic cracking?

options.text: Around 600 to 700 degrees Celsius
options.explanation: The spec wording fixes the range at 600-700 degrees, hot enough to vaporise the chains.

options.text: Around 100 to 200 degrees Celsius
options.explanation: That is far too cool to vaporise long chains and crack them.

options.text: Room temperature with a strong catalyst
options.explanation: No catalyst lets cracking run cold; heat is part of the condition set.

options.text: Above 2000 degrees Celsius
options.explanation: That overshoots the industrial range by far and wastes energy.

check.stem: What role does the hot powdered catalyst play in cracking?

options.text: Its surface provides the contact at which covalent bonds break
options.explanation: Molecules meeting the hot catalyst surface undergo the bond-breaking that splits them.

options.text: It dissolves the hydrocarbons into a solution
options.explanation: Nothing dissolves; the reaction happens on the solid surface in the vapour phase.

options.text: It burns the hydrocarbons to carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Cracking is decomposition, not burning; no oxygen takes part.

options.text: It cools the vapours to condense them
options.explanation: The catalyst is hot, not cold, and the products stay vapours until collected.

check.stem: Which product mixture does cracking deliver?

options.text: A mixture of shorter alkanes and alkenes
options.explanation: The random break-up yields both single-bonded alkanes and double-bonded alkenes.

options.text: Only alkanes, because the chains stay saturated
options.explanation: The double-bonded alkenes are a headline product of every cracking run.

options.text: Only alkenes, because all bonds break
options.explanation: Shorter alkanes always accompany the alkenes in the product mixture.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.explanation: Those are combustion products; cracking makes hydrocarbons, not oxides.

check.stem: Why are kerosene and diesel oil common feedstocks for cracking?

options.text: Because they are long-chain fractions often in surplus, unlike the petrol wanted
options.explanation: Surplus long chains are cracked into the short-chain petrol, alkenes and hydrogen in demand.

options.text: Because they are the only fractions that can vaporise
options.explanation: Any fraction vaporises at temperature; the choice is about surplus and demand.

options.text: Because they contain alkenes ready-made
options.explanation: They are alkane-rich; the alkenes are made by the cracking itself.

options.text: Because cracking cools them into petrol
options.explanation: Cooling collects products; it does not convert one fraction into another.

lessons.title: Supply, demand and the reason for cracking
sourceHeadings: Supply & demand of crude oil fractions
lessons.opening: The column delivers fractions in proportions geology chose, not proportions customers ordered. This lesson explains how the gap between supply and demand makes cracking necessary, with fuel oil as the classic example.
keyPoints: Supply is how much of a fraction refining the crude oil can produce.
Demand is how much of that fraction customers want to buy.
Demand for some fractions outstrips supply, so cracking converts excess fractions into more useful ones.
Fuel oil and bitumen sit in surplus, so they are cracked into the wanted petrol, kerosene and diesel.
Short-chain molecules such as petrol, kerosene and diesel are demanded more than their supply allows.

low.restatement: Refining makes too much of the long-chain fractions and not enough of the short ones people want. Cracking turns the surplus long chains into the missing short products.
low.analogy: It is a bakery with too many plain loaves and not enough sliced bread: the oven work called cracking converts the unpopular loaves into the style customers queue for.
low.examPointer: Answer why-is-cracking-necessary questions with both words: supply of long chains exceeds demand, demand for short chains exceeds supply.

medium.restatement: Each fraction has its own supply, fixed by what refining yields, and its own demand, set by what customers buy. Where demand for short-chain fractions outruns their supply, the surplus long-chain fractions such as fuel oil and bitumen are cracked into petrol, kerosene and diesel, rebalancing the ledger the column cannot fix by itself.
medium.analogy: The refinery runs a currency exchange between chain lengths: geology pays out heavy fractions nobody wants, and cracking is the exchange desk that converts them into the short-chain currency the market spends.
medium.examPointer: Name fuel oil and bitumen as the surplus examples, and quote the trio of wanted products, petrol, kerosene and diesel.

check.stem: What does supply mean in the fraction balance?

options.text: How much of a fraction refining the crude oil can produce
options.explanation: Supply is fixed by the refining yield of each chain-length group.

options.text: How much customers want to buy
options.explanation: That is demand; supply is the amount refining delivers.

options.text: How hot the column must be
options.explanation: Temperature is a process condition, not the supply quantity.

options.text: How much crude oil remains underground
options.explanation: Reserves are a separate idea; supply here means refining output.

check.stem: Why is cracking necessary for the fraction balance?

options.text: Because demand for some fractions outstrips their supply from refining
options.explanation: The gap between what refining yields and what customers want is closed by cracking surplus fractions.

options.text: Because supply and demand match perfectly for every fraction
options.explanation: If they matched, no cracking would ever be needed; the mismatch is the whole reason.

options.text: Because cracking makes fractions burn more cleanly
options.explanation: Cleaner burning is not the balancing mechanism; product mix is.

options.text: Because the column cannot run without cracking first
options.explanation: Distillation runs first and delivers the fractions; cracking comes after.

check.stem: Which fractions are described as surplus in this note?

options.text: Fuel oil and bitumen
options.explanation: The note names these heavy fractions as the surplus ones sent for cracking and modification.

options.text: Petrol and kerosene
options.explanation: Those are the short-chain products in demand, not the surplus feed.

options.text: Refinery gas and gasoline
options.explanation: Light fractions are demanded, not surplus; they are never the cracking feed here.

options.text: No fraction is ever surplus
options.explanation: The supply-demand chart shows clear surplus at the heavy end.

check.stem: Demand for short-chain hydrocarbons compared with their supply is best described as:

options.text: Greater demand than supply
options.explanation: The chart caption states demand for petrol, kerosene and diesel exceeds their supply.

options.text: Greater supply than demand
options.explanation: That is the heavy-fraction situation; the short chains run the other way.

options.text: Exactly equal
options.explanation: Equality would remove the need for cracking entirely.

options.text: Unmeasurable in principle
options.explanation: The supply-demand chart measures exactly this comparison.

check.stem: The exam hint reminds you that cracking is which type of energy change?

options.text: Endothermic, because breaking bonds needs heat input
options.explanation: Cracking absorbs the heat supplied by the hot conditions, classifying it as endothermic.

options.text: Exothermic, because the furnace feels hot
options.explanation: The furnace is hot because we heat it; the reaction itself takes heat in.

options.text: Neither, because no bonds are involved
options.explanation: Covalent bonds are broken, which is exactly why energy is absorbed.

options.text: Both, depending on the catalyst colour
options.explanation: Catalyst appearance has no bearing on the energy direction.

glossary.definition: An industrial process that breaks long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful alkane and alkene molecules.
A substance that speeds a reaction without being used up; cracking uses hot powdered alumina or silica.
Breaking a substance into simpler molecules using heat, as happens to hydrocarbons on the hot catalyst surface.
How much of a particular fraction can be produced from refining the crude oil.
How much of a fraction customers want to buy; short-chain fractions are demanded beyond their supply.
